title: Reproduction in Plants
seo_title: Primary 5 Science: Reproduction in Plants Worksheets (with Answers)
standard_code: Primary 5: Cycles in plants and animals (Reproduction in plants)
standard_text: Identify the parts of a flower and their functions in reproduction. Describe the processes of pollination, fertilisation (the fusion of the male and female reproductive cells), seed and fruit formation, and seed dispersal by wind, water, animals and splitting. Recognise that some plants reproduce by spores (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 5 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on reproduction in plants: flower parts, pollination, fertilisation, fruits and seeds, seed dispersal and spores. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: The ovule becomes a seed; the ovary becomes a fruit.
body_html:
How to think about it

Flowering plants reproduce by seeds.

  • Pollination: pollen moves from the anther to the stigma (by insects or wind).
  • Fertilisation: the male reproductive cell (from the pollen) joins the female reproductive cell in the ovule.
  • The ovule becomes a seed; the ovary becomes a fruit.
  • Seeds are dispersed by wind, water, animals or splitting, so new plants do not compete with the parent.
  • Ferns and mosses reproduce by spores.
Example

A flower is covered so no insects reach it. What happens?

No pollen reaches the stigma

No fertilisation

Answer: No fruit or seeds form.

Example

A coconut is found on a beach far from any tree. How did it get there?

Its husk traps air

It floats

Answer: By water.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up pollination and fertilisation. Pollination is the transfer of pollen; fertilisation is the joining of the reproductive cells.
  • Thinking the petals become the fruit. The ovary becomes the fruit.
  • Thinking the stigma makes pollen. The anther makes pollen.
  • Thinking all fruits are dispersed by animals. Look at the features: wings, husk, hooks or splitting pods.

faq.q: What is the difference between pollination and fertilisation?
faq.a: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. Fertilisation is the joining of the male and female reproductive cells in the ovule, which happens after pollination.

faq.q: Which part of the flower becomes the fruit?
faq.a: The ovary becomes the fruit, and the fertilised ovules inside it become the seeds.
By wind (light, with wings or hairs), by water (fibrous husk that floats), by animals (juicy fruits or hooks) and by splitting (dry fruits that burst open).

items.q: What does the petal of a flower do?
c: It contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.
It connects the stigma to the ovary.
It is often brightly coloured to attract insects.
items.e: The petal is often brightly coloured to attract insects.

items.q: Which part of a flower contains the ovules and becomes the fruit?
items.e: The ovary contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.

items.q: Is the anther part of the male or the female part of a flower?
items.e: The stamen (anther and filament) is male; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is female.

items.q: Is the stigma part of the male or the female part of a flower?
items.e: The stamen (anther and filament) is male; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is female.

items.q: Why is seed dispersal important?
c: Young plants grow away from the parent and do not compete for light, water and space.
It makes the parent plant bigger.
It stops the seeds from germinating.
items.e: Overcrowding means less light, water and space for each plant.

items.q: After fertilisation, what does the ovary develop into?
items.e: The ovules inside become the seeds.

items.q: What is the job of the ovary of a flower?
c: to hold the tiny ovules that become seeds
to give insects a sweet drink
to attract insects with their colour and scent
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: What is pollination?
c: the growth of a seed into a seedling
the joining of male and female reproductive cells
the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma
items.e: Pollination comes before fertilisation.

items.q: How do ferns and mosses reproduce?
items.e: Ferns make spores under their leaves.

items.q: Which part of a flower protects the flower when it is a bud?
items.e: The sepal protects the flower when it is a bud.

items.q: What is the job of the nectar of a flower?
c: to give insects a sweet drink
to protect the flower while it is a bud
to catch pollen with its sticky top
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: Which part of the flower is the male part?
items.e: The stamen is the anther and the filament.

items.q: What is the job of the petals of a flower?
c: to give insects a sweet drink
to catch pollen with its sticky top
to protect the flower while it is a bud
to attract insects with their colour and scent
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: What is fertilisation?
c: the joining of the male reproductive cell and the female reproductive cell
items.e: It takes place in the ovule.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to make pollen?
items.e: Each part of a flower helps make seeds.

items.q: What does the stigma of a flower do?
c: It contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.
It is often brightly coloured to attract insects.
It protects the flower when it is a bud.
It receives pollen; it is often sticky.
items.e: The stigma receives pollen; it is often sticky.

items.q: Which part of the flower is the female part?
items.e: The pistil is the stigma, style and ovary.

items.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
items.e: The anther makes pollen.

items.q: After fertilisation, what does the ovule develop into?
items.e: Each fertilised ovule becomes one seed.

items.q: What does the style of a flower do?
c: It connects the stigma to the ovary.
It is often brightly coloured to attract insects.
It contains the female reproductive cell and becomes the seed.
items.e: The style connects the stigma to the ovary.

items.q: A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule. What happened just before this?
c: The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants. What happened just before this?
c: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: A watermelon has many seeds. What does this tell us about its flower?
items.e: Each seed came from a fertilised ovule.

items.q: The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit. What happened just before this?
c: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: A flower has feathery stigmas that hang outside the flower. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: Why might a fruit tree in a greenhouse with no insects produce very few fruits?
items.e: Without pollination there is no fertilisation.

items.q: The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit. What happens next?
c: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination). What happens next?
c: The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: A flower has anthers that hang outside the flower on long filaments. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: Why do insect-pollinated flowers have nectar?
c: to attract insects, which pick up pollen while feeding
items.e: Insects carry pollen to other flowers.

items.q: Why do the petals of a flower wither after fertilisation?
c: They are no longer needed to attract insects.
items.e: The ovary grows into the fruit instead.

items.q: A flower has a sweet scent and nectar. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: A flower has small, dull petals and no scent. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: A flower has light, smooth pollen made in large amounts. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation). What happens next?
c: The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: A flower has sticky or spiky pollen grains. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers make light pollen that is blown about.

items.q: What does a pollen grain contain?
items.e: The female reproductive cell is in the ovule.

items.q: Which statement about pollination and fertilisation is correct?
items.e: Pollen must reach the stigma before fertilisation can happen.

items.q: Why do wind-pollinated flowers produce large amounts of pollen?
c: Most of the pollen is blown away and never reaches a stigma.
The pollen is food for insects.
items.e: Producing a lot increases the chance of pollination.

items.q: Which happens to the ovary wall as the fruit forms?
c: It becomes the seed coat only.
It falls off with the petals.
It grows and may become fleshy or dry.
items.e: Mangoes have fleshy fruit walls; balsam pods are dry.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the rubber tree dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the rubber tree: dry fruit that splits open with a pop. The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by water?
items.e: They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: Why are coconuts often found growing on beaches?
c: The fibrous husk traps air, so coconuts float and are carried by the sea.
items.e: Coconuts are dispersed by water.

items.q: Which feature would most help a fruit to float?
c: a fibrous husk with air spaces
a heavy, hard shell with no air
items.e: Trapped air makes the fruit float.

items.q: Why do seeds dispersed by animals often have juicy, brightly coloured fruits?
c: to attract animals to eat them
items.e: The seeds pass out in the animal's droppings far away.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by wind?
items.e: They are small and light, with wings or hairs.

items.q: A fruit has a dry fruit that splits open with a pop. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the saga dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the saga: pod that twists and splits open. The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: A fruit has a fibrous, spongy husk. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: Love grass seeds stick to your socks after a walk in a field. How are they dispersed?
items.e: The tiny hooks catch on fur and clothes.

items.q: Why do wind-dispersed seeds need to be light?
c: so that they can be carried far by the wind
items.e: Heavy seeds fall near the parent.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the sea almond dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the sea almond: fibrous, spongy husk. They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by animals?
items.e: They are juicy and eaten, or have hooks that catch on fur.

items.q: Why does a balsam fruit burst open when touched?
c: to fling its seeds away from the parent plant
items.e: This is dispersal by splitting (explosive action).

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by wind?
items.e: They are small and light, with wings or hairs.

items.q: A seed with wings fell 20 m from its parent tree. A seed of the same size without wings fell 3 m away. What does this show?
c: Wings help seeds to be carried further by the wind.
Seeds without wings are dispersed by animals.
items.e: Wings increase the surface area to catch the wind.

items.q: A fruit has a wing-like structures. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: They are small and light, with wings or hairs.

items.q: A fruit has a pod that twists and splits open. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the pong pong dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the pong pong: fibrous husk. They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by animals?
items.e: They are juicy and eaten, or have hooks that catch on fur.

items.q: Which condition helps spores to grow into new ferns?
c: a sealed dark box with no water
items.e: Ferns and mosses grow well in damp places.

items.q: Where are the spores of a fern found?
c: in spore cases on the underside of its leaves
items.e: The brown dots under fern leaves are spore cases.

items.q: A mango fruit has one seed. What does this tell us about its ovary?
c: Only one ovule developed into a seed.
The fruit grew from the stigma.
items.e: One fertilised ovule gives one seed.

items.q: Why do some plants make many seeds?
c: Many seeds may be eaten or land in poor places, so making many helps some survive.
Seeds are needed to make food.
items.e: Only some seeds land in good places to grow.

items.q: Which of these plants has its seeds dispersed by animals?
items.e: They are juicy and eaten, or have hooks that catch on fur.

items.q: Which of these plants does NOT produce flowers?
items.e: Ferns and mosses reproduce by spores.

items.q: Which part of the fruit protects the seeds?
c: the fruit wall, which develops from the ovary wall
items.e: The fruit protects the seeds and helps disperse them.

items.q: What does the filament of a flower do?
c: It receives pollen; it is often sticky.
It contains the ovules and becomes the fruit.
items.e: The filament holds up the anther.

items.q: What does the ovule of a flower do?
c: It is often brightly coloured to attract insects.
It contains the female reproductive cell and becomes the seed.
items.e: The ovule contains the female reproductive cell and becomes the seed.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the rambutan dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the rambutan: sweet, juicy flesh. They are juicy and eaten, or have hooks that catch on fur.

items.q: Which statement about pollen is correct?
c: It contains the female reproductive cell.
It is made in the ovary.
It is made in the anther and contains the male reproductive cell.
items.e: The ovule contains the female reproductive cell.

items.q: The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation). What happened just before this?
c: The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule.
The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

items.q: Which shows the correct order?
c: pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit formation → seed dispersal → germination
items.e: Each step needs the one before it.

items.q: A papaya fruit has hundreds of seeds. How many ovules were fertilised?
c: about the same number as the number of seeds
more than ten times the number of seeds
items.e: Each seed comes from one fertilised ovule.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the balsam dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the balsam: fruit that bursts open when touched. The dry fruit splits open and flings the seeds out.

items.q: A fruit has a spongy seed head. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: How are the seeds or fruits of the lotus dispersed?
items.e: Feature of the lotus: spongy seed head. They have a fibrous husk that traps air, so they float.

items.q: Which part of a flower receives pollen; it is often sticky?
items.e: The stigma receives pollen; it is often sticky.

items.q: Which part of a flower holds up the anther?
items.e: The filament holds up the anther.

items.q: A pollen tube grows down the style to the ovule. What happens next?
c: The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.
Pollen is carried from the anther to the stigma (pollination).
The seeds are dispersed and germinate into new plants.
The male reproductive cell joins with the female reproductive cell in the ovule (fertilisation).
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal → germination.

c: They had less competition for light, water and space.
items.e: Seeds near the parent are shaded.

items.q: Siti covered some hibiscus flowers with plastic bags before they opened. Why did these flowers produce no fruits?
c: Insects could not reach them, so they were not pollinated.
The bags made the petals fall.
items.e: No pollination means no fertilisation.

items.q: How could you investigate which seed design falls most slowly?
c: Throw them as hard as possible.
Drop model seeds with different wing sizes from the same height and time them.
items.e: Fair test.

items.q: A fruit has a wing-like structure. How is it most likely dispersed?
items.e: They are small and light, with wings or hairs.

items.q: Why is it a problem if bee numbers fall?
c: Fewer flowers would be pollinated, so fewer fruits and seeds would form.
items.e: Pollinators matter.

c: They release huge amounts of light pollen into the air.
items.e: Grass pollen.

items.q: Ravi removed the anthers from a flower and covered it. Why did it not develop into a fruit?
c: No pollen could reach the stigma.
items.e: Removing the anthers stops self-pollination.
